title: Course
text:
Audience and teaching approach
This course is designed for experienced working professionals. The instructor describes the cohort as having roughly 4–20 years of experience across fields including IT, finance and training. Students bring different kinds of professional expertise; the course does not assume a typical undergraduate background or identical prior knowledge.
The programme is intended to deepen students’ mastery of AI and data science, including agentic AI. Lessons begin with a practical problem before formal definitions. In the first probability lecture, students consider an LLM triage audit of six tickets, including one that requires both Billing and Account Support. Historical interpretations of probability lead to a set-based model for uniformly selecting one ticket ID. The example develops events, their probabilities, and an indicator random variable through its image and inverse image. A separate Gamma model for closure time shows how continuous probabilities are calculated by integration. Worked examples connect calculations to their assumptions and limits. Contexts vary across AI, engineering, IT, finance and training; hypothetical values are identified as such.
For each topic, students identify the quantity or event of interest, examine the available information, calculate under stated assumptions, and then study the formal definition. Lessons include many short, tractable problems with worked solutions so students can build fluency at a measured pace. Course prose is factual and formal, without aphorisms or dramatic framing.

2. Historical interpretations of probability
Probability has been interpreted in several ways. The accounts below answer different questions about what the number 4/64/6 might mean. None follows just from seeing six rows in a table.

Classical equal-likelihood
The classical rule counts favourable outcomes among equally likely cases. If one ticket ID is selected uniformly from the six IDs, four selections produce agreement, so
P(agreement)=46=23.P(\text{agreement})=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
This calculation is valid for that selection experiment. It does not imply that future tickets are equally likely to be any of these six records, or that the six records represent future traffic. A finite list defines possible cases; the uniform selection rule supplies the equal weights.
The partition chosen for counting also matters. Group the tickets by the pair (reviewer outcome, model classification):

There are four occupied pair types in this audit. If an experiment selected one of these four types uniformly, two of the four would be exact matches, giving 2/42/4. If it selected one of the six ticket IDs uniformly, the pair types would instead have probabilities 1/6,2/6,2/6,1/61/6,2/6,2/6,1/6, giving 4/64/6. Thresholding two destination scores separately permits four model outputs: neither, Billing only, Account Support only, or both. Thus the full product contains 4×4=164\times4=16 reviewer/model pairs, of which four occur in this audit. Uniform selection among all 16 pairs would be a third experiment; its four matching pairs would give agreement probability 4/16=1/44/16=1/4. Equal weighting of pair types does not follow from grouping tickets that way. Counting requires a stated set of cases and a reason to treat those cases as equally likely.


Frequency
The observed agreement proportion is
p̂6=16∑i=16Ii=46,\widehat p_6=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{6}I_i=\frac{4}{6},
where Ii=1I_i=1 when the model classification exactly matches the reviewer’s reference outcome for ticket tit_i, and Ii=0I_i=0 otherwise. A frequency interpretation connects a probability to the limiting relative frequency in a specified repeatable process. This audit records one finite set of six tickets; it does not establish that limit or show that future ticket mix and model performance will remain the same.
Repeatedly sampling the LLM for the same text under randomized decoding would define another process. Its output frequency would describe generated classifications, not necessarily agreement with reviewer decisions. The process and event must be stated before interpreting a frequency.


Subjective probability and Bayesian updating
A subjective interpretation treats probability as a person’s degree of belief given available information. An analyst might assess the chance that the model agrees with the review protocol on a future ticket, using this audit and other stated information. The six rows do not determine that assessment uniquely. Coherence constrains probability assignments; subjective does not mean arbitrary. Countable additivity is an additional condition in the Kolmogorov model and does not follow from every finite coherence argument.
Bayesian updating describes how an assessment changes when evidence is observed. If HH is the proposition that the next ticket’s model classification will agree with its reference outcome and DD is additional evidence, Bayes’ rule gives
P(H∣D)=P(D∣H)P(H)P(D),P(D)>0.P(H\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid H)P(H)}{P(D)},\qquad P(D)>0.
The formula does not supply the prior or likelihood; those come from a model and stated information. Conditional probability and Bayesian updating will be developed later.


Logical or evidential probability
A logical or evidential interpretation aims to quantify how strongly stated evidence supports a proposition. Here the evidence could include the six audit rows, the review protocol and assumptions about the future ticket population. A numerical answer requires a rule connecting that evidence and those assumptions to a degree of support. If the rule invokes indifference, it must specify which cases are treated equally and why. Counting ticket IDs and counting occupied label-pair types give different answers because they describe different selection rules. This identifies a problem with an unspecified indifference rule; it does not refute every logical account.


What the interpretations leave for a probability model
Classical probability emphasizes equal likelihood, frequency emphasizes repetition, subjective probability represents an assessment given information, and logical accounts specify evidential support. A propensity account would treat the configured randomized generation process as the chance-producing mechanism. These accounts differ in interpretation. A mathematical calculation also needs the possible outcomes, the event of interest and a probability assignment. The next example shows why the sampling procedure is part of that specification.
Checkpoint 2. For each interpretation, state what additional assumption or information is needed to use it for a claim about future tickets.

section: 3. A second question: Bertrand’s random chord
text:
3. A second question: Bertrand’s random chord
Draw an equilateral triangle inside a circle. Consider the question:

If a chord is selected at random from the circle, what is the probability that its length exceeds the side length of the triangle?

The phrase “selected at random” does not specify how the chord is generated. Bertrand described different sampling procedures for chords, which give 1/31/3, 1/21/2 and 1/41/4 for the same length comparison. These values follow from different probability distributions induced by the respective sampling procedures; the problem statement alone does not say which procedure to use. John D. Norton’s University of Pittsburgh page presents the three sampling arguments and their values.
The procedures are: choose two independent uniform endpoints (1/31/3); choose a uniform radial distance and an independent uniform direction (1/21/2); or choose a midpoint uniformly in disk area (1/41/4). These are different models. We will not choose among them or derive the answers in this section. The example identifies information a probability question can leave unspecified: the outcomes and, especially, the sampling rule that determines their probabilities.

Kolmogorov’s set-based framework
Kolmogorov’s axiomatic framework gives probability a mathematical foundation in terms of sets and a measure. Its three objects are written
(Ω,ℱ,P).(\Omega,\mathcal F,P).
Here Ω\Omega is the sample space of possible outcomes, ℱ\mathcal F is the collection of events to which probabilities are assigned, and P:ℱ→[0,1]P:\mathcal F\to[0,1] is the probability measure. The event collection has closure requirements, and the measure obeys nonnegativity, normalization and countable additivity. We will define and apply each object using the ticket audit. The supplement returns to Bertrand’s question and specifies the sampling models in full.

\;X_B(t_5)=1,\;X_B(t_6)=0.
A real-valued random variable is a measurable function from outcomes to real numbers, X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R. We explain measurability below using inverse images. Its input is an individual outcome. In contrast, a set function has sets as inputs: the probability measure takes an event EE and returns P(E)P(E). Having a set as its domain does not make every function a set function. Once the outcome is specified, the function’s value is fixed. It is not a random mechanism and it is not the probability measure. In this experiment, the ticket ID is selected at random; XBX_B records whether its reviewer reference includes Billing.

Image: values produced by a set of outcomes
For E⊆ΩE\subseteq\Omega, the image of EE under XBX_B is
XB(E)={XB(t):t∈E}.X_B(E)=\{X_B(t):t\in E\}.
For the Account Support event A={t1,t3,t6}A=\{t_1,t_3,t_6\}, t1t_1 also requires Billing, while t3t_3 and t6t_6 do not. Hence
XB(A)={0,1}.X_B(A)=\{0,1\}.
This is a set of numerical values, not an event in the ticket sample space.


Inverse image: outcomes that produce selected values
For D⊆ℝD\subseteq\mathbb R, the inverse image is
XB−1(D)={t∈Ω:XB(t)∈D}.X_B^{-1}(D)=\{t\in\Omega:X_B(t)\in D\}.
In particular,
XB−1({1})={t1,t2,t5}=B,X_B^{-1}(\{1\})=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}=B,
and
XB−1({0})={t3,t4,t6}=Bc.X_B^{-1}(\{0\})=\{t_3,t_4,t_6\}=B^c.
An inverse image is a set of outcomes; it need not be an inverse function. The inverse image connects a numerical condition on a random variable to an event to which the probability measure applies:
P(XB=1)=P(XB−1({1}))=P(B)=36=12.P(X_B=1)=P\bigl(X_B^{-1}(\{1\})\bigr)=P(B)=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12.
The distribution of XBX_B is P(XB=1)=1/2P(X_B=1)=1/2 and P(XB=0)=1/2P(X_B=0)=1/2. The function XBX_B, its inverse-image event BB, and the number P(B)P(B) are three different objects.


Measurability and the probability law
To calculate P(XB∈D)P(X_B\in D), the inverse image XB−1(D)X_B^{-1}(D) must be an event. For example, XB−1((1/2,3/2))=B∈ℱX_B^{-1}((1/2,3/2))=B\in\mathcal F, giving probability 1/21/2. This requirement motivates the formal definition.
The Borel sigma-algebra ℬ(ℝ)\mathcal B(\mathbb R) is the smallest sigma-algebra containing all open intervals. It includes intervals, singletons and their countable unions, intersections and complements. A function X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R is measurable, and hence a real-valued random variable on (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), if
X−1(D)∈ℱfor every D∈ℬ(ℝ).X^{-1}(D)\in\mathcal F\quad\text{for every }D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
Its law or distribution is the probability measure
PX(D)=P(X−1(D)),D∈ℬ(ℝ).P_X(D)=P(X^{-1}(D)),\qquad D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
In the full finite model every function is measurable because all subsets are events. For XBX_B, the inverse image is one of ⌀,B,Bc,Ω\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega according to whether DD contains neither of 0 and 1, only 1, only 0, or both. Thus XBX_B is measurable even for the smaller collection 𝒢\mathcal G. Its law assigns mass 1/21/2 each to 0 and 1. By contrast, the ID-code function J(ti)=iJ(t_i)=i is not measurable for 𝒢\mathcal G: J−1({1})={t1}J^{-1}(\{1\})=\{t_1\} is unavailable in that collection. It is measurable for 2Ω2^\Omega.


Worked check: a die outcome and its numerical value
Roll a stipulated fair die once. Take Ωd={1,2,3,4,5,6}\Omega_d=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}, ℱd=2Ωd\mathcal F_d=2^{\Omega_d} and Pd(E)=|E|/6P_d(E)=|E|/6. Define Z(ω)=ωZ(\omega)=\omega. If face 4 occurs, distinguish the outcome 44, the singleton event {4}\{4\}, the function value Z(4)=4Z(4)=4, and the probability Pd({4})=1/6P_d(\{4\})=1/6. Also Z−1({2,4,6})={2,4,6}Z^{-1}(\{2,4,6\})=\{2,4,6\}, so Pd(Z is even)=1/2P_d(Z\text{ is even})=1/2. The identical numerals in this identity function do not identify its values with their probabilities.

7. A continuous example: ticket closure time
The triplet is often not written out in routine probability calculations. To see what remains implicit, consider a ticket selected from a specified service process, and let TcT_c be its closure time, measured in hours. The question

What is the probability that this ticket takes more than one day to close?

is written P(Tc>24)P(T_c>24), since one day is 24 hours. In an underlying ticket-system experiment, each outcome ω\omega determines a closure time Tc(ω)T_c(\omega) in hours. The event of interest is the inverse image
Tc−1((24,∞))={ω∈Ω:Tc(ω)>24}.T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=\{\omega\in\Omega:T_c(\omega)>24\}.
For an illustrative calculation, suppose the closure time follows a Gamma distribution with shape α=2\alpha=2 and scale θ=12\theta=12 hours. These are hypothetical model parameters, not estimates from the six-ticket audit. Under the shape-scale parameterization, the density is
fTc(t)=tα−1e−t/θΓ(α)θα,t≥0.f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t/\theta}}
{\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha},\qquad t\geq 0.
Here α,θ>0\alpha,\theta>0 and Γ(a)=∫0∞ua−1e−udu\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}du for a>0a>0; in particular, Γ(2)=1\Gamma(2)=1. With α=2\alpha=2 and θ=12\theta=12 hours, this becomes
fTc(t)=t122e−t/12,t≥0,f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t}{12^2}e^{-t/12},\qquad t\geq0,
where tt is measured in hours. Here α\alpha is the shape parameter, not the mean. The mean in this shape-scale parameterization is E[Tc]=αθ=24E[T_c]=\alpha\theta=24 hours. The plotted curve shows this model and shades the area to the right of the 24-hour cutoff, which coincides with the mean.



Gamma density for ticket closure time TcT_c under the illustrative model. The vertical line marks both the mean and the 24-hour cutoff; the shaded right tail represents P(Tc>24 h)P(T_c>24\text{ h}).


For the six-ticket experiment above, probabilities were calculated by counting equally likely IDs: P(C)=|C|/6P(C)=|C|/6. A continuous ticket time cannot be handled by counting individual possible durations. Under a density model, the probability of an interval is the area under the density over that interval. A density value is not itself a probability; integration accumulates the density across the range. In the audit model, the corresponding finite calculation is a sum of singleton probabilities; for example, P(C)=∑ti∈CP({ti})=4/6P(C)=\sum_{t_i\in C}P(\{t_i\})=4/6. The closure-time probability is the integral of its density over the event. With the substitution u=t/12u=t/12,
P(Tc>24)=∫24∞t144e−t/12dt=∫2∞ue−udu=[−(u+1)e−u]2∞=(2+1)e−2=3e−2≈0.406.\begin{aligned}
P(T_c>24)
&=\int_{24}^{\infty}\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12}\,dt\\
&=\int_{2}^{\infty}u e^{-u}\,du\\
&=\left[-(u+1)e^{-u}\right]_2^\infty\\
&=(2+1)e^{-2}=3e^{-2}\approx0.406.
\end{aligned}
Thus, under this stipulated model, the probability that closure takes more than 24 hours is about 0.4060.406. A different shape, scale or target ticket population would give a different value. Specifying the Gamma family alone would not suffice; the parameters and their parameterization are needed.

What a probability density specifies
The calculation above uses an area, not a density height. Formally, a random variable TT has a probability density function ff if ff is nonnegative and measurable, ∫ℝf(t)dt=1\int_{\mathbb R}f(t)\,dt=1, and
P(T∈D)=∫Df(t)dtfor every Borel set D.P(T\in D)=\int_D f(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every Borel set }D.
Here f(t)=0f(t)=0 for t<0t<0. The same substitution checks normalization: ∫0∞(t/144)e−t/12dt=∫0∞ue−udu=1\int_0^\infty (t/144)e^{-t/12}dt=\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}du=1. A singleton has zero area, so P(Tc=24)=0P(T_c=24)=0, while a range can have positive probability. Not every random variable has a density; the Billing indicator has a discrete law.


The triplet for the closure-time model
For this calculation, use the following canonical probability space, which models closure time alone:
(Ωc,ℱc,Pc).(\Omega_c,\mathcal F_c,P_c).
In the calculation above, the shorthand P(Tc>24)P(T_c>24) denotes Pc(Tc>24)P_c(T_c>24) on this space. It is distinct from PP, the uniform measure used for selecting one of the six audited ticket IDs.

Sample space: Ωc=[0,∞)\Omega_c=[0,\infty), the possible closure durations measured in hours.
Event collection: ℱc=ℬ([0,∞))\mathcal F_c=\mathcal B([0,\infty)), the Borel subsets of the nonnegative real line: sets obtained by intersecting Borel subsets of ℝ\mathbb R with [0,∞)[0,\infty).
Probability measure: for every E∈ℱcE\in\mathcal F_c,
Pc(E)=∫EfTc(t)dt,fTc(t)=t144e−t/12,t≥0.P_c(E)=\int_E f_{T_c}(t)\,dt,
\qquad f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12},\quad t\geq0.

The density integrates to one, so Pc(Ωc)=1P_c(\Omega_c)=1. Define the random variable by Tc:Ωc→[0,∞)T_c:\Omega_c\to[0,\infty), Tc(t)=tT_c(t)=t. Thus the event of closure after 24 hours is
Tc−1((24,∞))=(24,∞)∈ℱc,T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=(24,\infty)\in\mathcal F_c,
and its probability is
Pc(Tc>24)=Pc((24,∞))=∫24∞fTc(t)dt.P_c(T_c>24)=P_c((24,\infty))
=\int_{24}^{\infty}f_{T_c}(t)\,dt.
This is one explicit probability space realizing the assumed Gamma law. A full ticket-system model could use outcomes that also include ticket type, priority and other information, with closure time as a function on that larger space. In routine calculations, Tc∼Gamma⁡(shape 2,scale 12 h)T_c\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape }2,\text{scale }12\text{ h}) states the induced law needed for probabilities about closure time without writing the whole triplet. The distribution of TcT_c does not by itself describe every other random quantity in the ticket system.
This is why many engineering and AI calculations work directly with random variables and their distributions after the probability-space foundation has been established.

Problem 1: probability of “Other”
Find the probability that a uniformly selected ticket has neither Billing nor Account Support required according to the reviewer.
Solution. By definition, O=(B∪A)c={t4}O=(B\cup A)^c=\{t_4\}. Therefore
P(O)=16.P(O)=\frac{1}{6}.


Problem 2: exactly one named destination is required
Find the event and probability that exactly one of Billing and Account Support is required.
Solution. The event is
(B\A)∪(A\B)={t2,t3,t5,t6}. (B\setminus A)\cup(A\setminus B)=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}.
Its probability is 4/6=2/34/6=2/3.


Problem 3: agreement between reviewer and model
Let M(t)M(t) be the model’s classification and R(t)R(t) the reviewer’s reference classification for ticket tt. Define exact agreement as equality of these classification sets. The agreement event from the table is
C={t2,t3,t5,t6}.C=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}.
Under uniform selection, P(C)=4/6=2/3P(C)=4/6=2/3. This equals the observed agreement fraction because the experiment selects uniformly from this exact audit.


Problem 4: use an inverse image
Define Y(t)=1Y(t)=1 if the model classification exactly matches the reviewer and Y(t)=0Y(t)=0 otherwise. Then Y−1({1})=CY^{-1}(\{1\})=C, and
P(Y=1)=P(C)=46=23.P(Y=1)=P(C)=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
The random variable records an outcome numerically; its inverse image gives the event; the probability measure assigns that event a number.


Problem 5: change the audit selection weights
In a hypothetical follow-up experiment, select the same six IDs with stipulated weights (1,1,1,3,1,1)/8(1,1,1,3,1,1)/8. Keep Ω\Omega, its full power set and the labels fixed. Find the probabilities of agreement and Other.
Solution. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one, defining Q(E)=∑ti∈EwiQ(E)=\sum_{t_i\in E}w_i. Therefore Q(C)=(1+1+1+1)/8=1/2Q(C)=(1+1+1+1)/8=1/2 and Q(O)=3/8Q(O)=3/8. The observed fraction remains 4/64/6, but the selection probability changes. These weights specify an exercise, not an estimate of future traffic.


Problem 6: fraud-screen flags
A hypothetical fixed review batch has 20 transaction IDs. Reviewers label 4 as fraudulent. A screen flags 5: 3 of the 4 reviewer-positive transactions and 2 reviewer-negative transactions. Select one ID uniformly. Find the false-positive and false-negative events’ probabilities.
Solution. On Ω={1,…,20}\Omega=\{1,\ldots,20\} with its power set and uniform measure, write FF for flagged IDs and HH for reviewer-positive IDs. Then |F∩Hc|=2|F\cap H^c|=2 and |Fc∩H|=1|F^c\cap H|=1, so their probabilities are 2/20=0.102/20=0.10 and 1/20=0.051/20=0.05. Among the 16 reviewer-negative records, the false-positive fraction is instead 2/16=0.1252/16=0.125. That changes the denominator and the selection experiment; it is not the probability just calculated.


Problem 7: sensor tolerance
For a hypothetical engineering model, a sensor error EE is uniform on [−2,2][-2,2] millimetres. Use this interval as the sample space, its Borel sets as events, and density f(e)=1/4f(e)=1/4 on the interval. What is the probability of exceeding a tolerance of 1 mm in absolute value?
Solution. The error is the identity random variable. The failure event is [−2,−1)∪(1,2][-2,-1)\cup(1,2], of total length 2, giving P(|E|>1)=∫[−2,−1)∪(1,2](1/4)de=1/2P(|E|>1)=\int_{[-2,-1)\cup(1,2]}(1/4)de=1/2. Exact boundary values have probability zero under this model. Uniform error is stipulated, not established by the tolerance specification.


Problem 8: assessment pass indicator
Select one of five hypothetical assessment records uniformly. Their fixed scores are 45, 60, 70, 80 and 95; the pass threshold is 60 inclusive. Specify a random variable and its law for the pass/fail result.
Solution. Outcomes are record IDs a1,…,a5a_1,\ldots,a_5, with the power set and singleton weights 1/51/5. Set Y(ai)=𝟏{score≥60}Y(a_i)=\mathbf1_{\{\text{score}\ge60\}}. Then Y−1({1})={a2,a3,a4,a5}Y^{-1}(\{1\})=\{a_2,a_3,a_4,a_5\}, PY({1})=4/5P_Y(\{1\})=4/5 and PY({0})=1/5P_Y(\{0\})=1/5. This is a probability under selection from these records; it does not establish a future cohort’s pass rate.

9. Connection to AI evaluation and continuation
The probability 2/32/3 here concerns uniform selection from six audited ticket IDs. It is not automatically the model’s agreement probability on future traffic. That requires a defined target population, an appropriate sampling process and assumptions connecting this audit to future tickets. Changing the reviewer protocol may also change the event called “agreement.”
The same distinctions arise in AI evaluation. A test-set accuracy is an observed proportion. Interpreting it as a probability of correct classification for future cases requires additional assumptions. If model generation is stochastic, its repeated-output distribution is another probability model with a different outcome space. In each case, specify the outcomes, event and sampling or generation process before interpreting a probability.
A suitable first stopping point is the calculation of P(B∪A)=5/6P(B\cup A)=5/6 at the end of Section 4. Continue to the triplet, sigma-algebra and axioms once the class can identify the complement event OO. The random-variable and image sections can continue in a later meeting. Bertrand’s chord problem is posed here but not derived; the rigorous supplement specifies its sampling models and works through their parametrizations and probabilities.

01.1 main materials
Supplementary materials
This supplement gives the formal definitions, parametrizations and derivations supporting the main lecture. Its details are intended for supplementary study alongside the corresponding lecture topics. For the chord calculations, RR is the fixed circle radius, TT the normalized midpoint distance, and LL the chord length, as in the Bertrand deck. The Billing indicator in the main notes remains XBX_B.
The main lecture motivates these constructions with questions about a hypothetical six-ticket routing audit, before introducing formal probability spaces. The proofs below do not depend on that application; they state the general hypotheses needed for the results.
Reference: Krishna Jagannathan, Probability Foundations for Electrical Engineers, 9 July 2025, Chapters 1, 4 and 11, particularly Definitions 68–70 for measurable functions, random variables and their laws. The calculations of the sampling maps are written out below.
A sample space is required to satisfy two conditions. It must be exhaustive, so that at least one of its elements occurs in any realization of the experiment, and its elements must be mutually exclusive, so that at most one of them occurs. Together these state that exactly one ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega occurs each time the experiment is performed.
Distinct outcomes correspond to disjoint singleton subsets. When these singletons belong to the event collection, they are singleton events:
{ω1}∩{ω2}=⌀whenever ω1≠ω2.\{\omega_1\}\cap\{\omega_2\}=\varnothing\quad\text{whenever }\omega_1\ne\omega_2 .
For countable Ω\Omega the singletons therefore form a countable disjoint partition, Ω=⋃ω∈Ω{ω}\Omega=\bigcup_{\omega\in\Omega}\{\omega\} (a disjoint union).
Outcomes are mutually exclusive; events need not be. For a single roll of a die, Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}, and the outcomes 22 and 44 cannot both occur. The events
A={2,4,6}(even),B={4,5,6}(greater than 3)A=\{2,4,6\}\ \text{(even)},\qquad B=\{4,5,6\}\ \text{(greater than 3)}
can both occur, since A∩B={4,6}≠⌀A\cap B=\{4,6\}\ne\varnothing.

title: 01.1 supplement · Sets, measurable maps and Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Consequences for calculation
The two cases are handled by different rules, and the distinction above is what separates them.
Because singletons are disjoint, countable additivity applies directly to them, and for a countable event AA whose singletons are measurable
P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω}).P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}).
For two events no such rule is available, since additivity requires disjointness. The correction term is the shared part:
P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
Writing P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B) for the die events above would count the outcomes 44 and 66 twice.


Two errors that this distinction prevents
A list of events is not a sample space. For one roll of a die, the pair “even” and “greater than 3” is not a sample space: both can occur in a single roll, so the second condition fails. They are events in the finer space {1,…,6}\{1,\ldots,6\}.
A valid sample space need not have equally likely elements. For two independent fair tosses, the list “a head on the first toss”, “a tail then a head”, “two tails” is exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so it is a legitimate sample space. Its members carry probabilities 1/21/2, 1/41/4 and 1/41/4: they group the equally likely ordered outcomes as {HH,HT}\{HH,HT\}, {TH}\{TH\} and {TT}\{TT\}. This calculation also appears in the interpretations deck. Mutual exclusivity is a requirement on the sample space; it says nothing about the probabilities assigned to its elements, and counting the members is valid only when they happen to be equally probable.


The same reading in the Bertrand construction
The sampling procedures in Section 3 produce a geometric chord almost surely. After excluding the stated null cases, we may describe their outputs on the common space 𝒞*\mathcal C_* of nondegenerate, nondiameter chords. In this output description, a chord is an elementary outcome. The three rotationally invariant models use the same chord space and event collection but different probability measures. Their original sampling outcomes can instead be angles, distances or points; Section 3 distinguishes these descriptions.
The event E={c:L(c)>3R}E=\{c:L(c)>\sqrt3R\} is not an outcome. It is a set containing uncountably many chords, and it is assigned a probability as a set.
This last point also marks the limit of the summation rule above. In a continuous model each individual outcome has probability zero, so
∑c∈EP({c})=0≠P(E),\sum_{c\in E}P(\{c\})=0\ne P(E),
and the probability of EE cannot be recovered by adding the probabilities of the outcomes it contains. Countable additivity is additivity over countably many disjoint events, and EE is not a countable union of its singletons. The rule P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω})P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}) applies to countable events with measurable singletons; it does not extend to an uncountable event by countable additivity.

2. Random variables, inverse images and probability laws
On a probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), a real-valued random variable is a measurable function
X:Ω→ℝ.X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R.
Measurability means that X−1(B)∈ℱX^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F for every Borel set B∈ℬ(ℝ)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R). The Borel σ-algebra is generated by open intervals and includes the intervals, singleton sets and their countable combinations used here. For a real-valued function, it is sufficient to check {ω:X(ω)≤x}∈ℱ\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\}\in\mathcal F for every real xx.

The distinction between a random variable and a set function
A random variable is a function on outcomes, not a real-valued set function on events. It induces the following map between collections of sets:
X−1:ℬ(ℝ)→ℱ,B↦{ω:X(ω)∈B}.X^{-1}:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad
B\longmapsto\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
The probability measure and the distribution of XX are real-valued set functions:
P:ℱ→[0,1],PX:ℬ(ℝ)→[0,1],P:\mathcal F\to[0,1],\qquad P_X:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\to[0,1],

3. Bertrand’s paradox: sampling maps and induced distributions
This section develops the Bertrand question posed in Section 3 of the main notes. What is the probability that a randomly generated chord is longer than the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle? We first calculate three answers to this same plain-English question. Only then do we use the Kolmogorov triplet to identify precisely which probability problem each calculation answers.

The paradox: one question, three answers
For the unit circle, a chord at distance rr from the centre has length
L=21−r2.L=2\sqrt{1-r^2}.
Thus L>3L>\sqrt3 exactly when r<1/2r<1/2, or equivalently when the chord intersects the interior of the concentric disk of radius 1/21/2.
Consider three plausible readings of “choose a chord at random.”

Choose its angle uniformly at a fixed endpoint. Fix a=(1,0)a=(1,0) and measure an angle θ∈(0,π)\theta\in(0,\pi) from the upward tangent towards the disk. The resulting chord has length 2sin⁡θ2\sin\,\theta. It is longer than 3\sqrt3 when π/3<θ<2π/3\pi/3<\theta<2\pi/3, an interval occupying one third of the available angular range. The answer is 1/31/3.
Choose its distance from the centre uniformly. Fix the midpoint direction and choose its distance rr uniformly between 0 and 1. Draw the chord perpendicular to that radius. The favorable distances satisfy r<1/2r<1/2, half the available range. The answer is 1/21/2.
Choose its midpoint uniformly in disk area. Draw the chord perpendicular to the radius through the chosen midpoint. It is long enough exactly when the midpoint lies inside the concentric disk of radius 1/21/2. That disk occupies one quarter of the total area. The answer is 1/41/4. The centre and boundary are zero-area exceptions handled below.

We have asked the same question in words and obtained
13,12,14.\frac13,\qquad\frac12,\qquad\frac14.
Each calculation is correct for its construction. The phrase “a random chord” leaves the sampling rule unspecified: uniform angle, distance and area are different assumptions. We now use the Kolmogorov triplet to resolve the apparent contradiction.


Making the experiments precise with the Kolmogorov triplet
A probability model is a triplet (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P): Ω\Omega specifies the outcomes, ℱ\mathcal F specifies the measurable events, and PP assigns their probabilities. We now identify these three components for each calculation. We distinguish the common geometric question from the event that represents it in each sampling space.
Experiment I: a uniform angle at a fixed endpoint. Fix the endpoint a=(1,0)a=(1,0). From the upward tangent at aa, measure θ∈(0,π)\theta\in(0,\pi) towards the interior of the disk. The ray has direction (−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)(-\sin\,\theta,\cos\,\theta); its second intersection with the circle defines the chord. Choose θ\theta uniformly. The triplet and measure are

P_1(B)=\frac1\pi\int_B d\theta\quad(B\in\mathcal F_1).
Here ℬ\mathcal B is the Borel σ-algebra, generated by the open subsets of the stated domain. The favorable event and probability are
E1=(π/3,2π/3),P1(E1)=2π/3−π/3π=13.E_1=(\pi/3,2\pi/3),\qquad P_1(E_1)=\frac{2\pi/3-\pi/3}{\pi}=\frac13.

Experiment II: a uniform distance with a fixed direction. Choose r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) uniformly, set the midpoint to (r,0)(r,0), and draw the vertical chord through it. Specifying the midpoint direction makes the chord unique; distance alone determines only its length.

Advanced: measures on a common chord space
The triplets above complete the resolution. The remaining calculations study sampling maps and induced measures on geometric chords. They are not needed to resolve the paradox.
We consider three rotationally invariant models independently:

Model A: choose two independent uniform endpoints on the circumference.
Model B: choose a uniform radial distance and an independent uniform midpoint direction.
Model C: choose a midpoint uniformly in disk area.

When f:𝖲→𝖸f:\mathsf S\to\mathsf Y is a bijection, f−1(y)f^{-1}(y) denotes an element of 𝖲\mathsf S, the value of the inverse function at yy. For any subset B⊆𝖸B\subseteq\mathsf Y, the notation f−1(B)f^{-1}(B) denotes a subset of 𝖲\mathsf S, the inverse image. The latter is defined even when ff is not one-to-one. In the Bertrand construction, CC and each Ψj\Psi_j are bijections on the stated restricted domains, whereas the chord-length function LL is not one-to-one.

5. Why a rotation-invariant probability cannot measure every subset
The main notes use Borel sets for the continuous model. Why not simply use every subset, as in the finite audit? Under the axiom of choice, the following construction shows that a normalized, countably additive, rotation-invariant probability on a circle cannot be defined on all its subsets.

The setting
Let Ω=[0,1)\Omega=[0,1) and define addition modulo 11,
x⊕y={x+y,x+y<1,x+y−1,x+y≥1,x\oplus y=\begin{cases}x+y,&x+y<1,\\x+y-1,&x+y\ge1,\end{cases}
with ⊖\ominus the corresponding subtraction. Under ⊕\oplus the set [0,1)[0,1) is an abelian group; identifying 00 with 11 makes it a circle, and x↦x⊕tx\mapsto x\oplus t is a rotation. For A⊆[0,1)A\subseteq[0,1) write A⊕t={a⊕t:a∈A}A\oplus t=\{a\oplus t:a\in A\}.
Suppose PP assigns a nonnegative real number to every subset of [0,1)[0,1) and satisfies

P([0,1))=1P([0,1))=1;
countable additivity;
rotation invariance: P(A⊕t)=P(A)P(A\oplus t)=P(A) for all AA and all t∈[0,1)t\in[0,1).



The construction
Let ℚ0=ℚ∩[0,1)\mathbb Q_0=\mathbb Q\cap[0,1), a countable subgroup of ([0,1),⊕)([0,1),\oplus). Define x∼yx\sim y when x⊖y∈ℚ0x\ominus y\in\mathbb Q_0. This is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the cosets x⊕ℚ0x\oplus\mathbb Q_0.
By the axiom of choice, let V⊆[0,1)V\subseteq[0,1) contain exactly one element of each class.
Claim 1: the sets V⊕qV\oplus q, for q∈ℚ0q\in\mathbb Q_0, are pairwise disjoint. Suppose v1⊕q1=v2⊕q2v_1\oplus q_1=v_2\oplus q_2 with v1,v2∈Vv_1,v_2\in V. Then v1⊖v2=q2⊖q1∈ℚ0v_1\ominus v_2=q_2\ominus q_1\in\mathbb Q_0, so v1∼v2v_1\sim v_2. Since VV has one element per class, v1=v2v_1=v_2, and therefore q1=q2q_1=q_2.
Claim 2: these sets cover [0,1)[0,1). Given x∈[0,1)x\in[0,1), let v∈Vv\in V be the representative of the class of xx. Then q=x⊖v∈ℚ0q=x\ominus v\in\mathbb Q_0 and x=v⊕q∈V⊕qx=v\oplus q\in V\oplus q.
So [0,1)[0,1) is the union of countably many pairwise disjoint sets, each a rotation of VV.


The contradiction
Write c=P(V)c=P(V). Rotation invariance gives P(V⊕q)=cP(V\oplus q)=c for every qq, and countable additivity applied to the countable disjoint family of Claim 1, whose union is [0,1)[0,1) by Claim 2, gives
1=P([0,1))=∑q∈ℚ0P(V⊕q)=∑q∈ℚ0c.1=P([0,1))=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q_0}P(V\oplus q)=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q_0}c .
Since PP is nonnegative, c≥0c\ge0. If c=0c=0 the right-hand side is 00; if c>0c>0 the sum diverges. Neither equals 11, so no such PP exists.
Moreover, if VV were Lebesgue measurable, each V⊕qV\oplus q would be measurable with the same Lebesgue measure: addition modulo 1 is an ordinary translation on each of two pieces. The same countable sum would then contradict the Lebesgue measure of [0,1)[0,1) being 1. Thus VV is not Lebesgue measurable. This is the Vitali construction on the circle.


Scope of the conclusion
The contradiction uses both countable additivity and rotation invariance. Finite additivity alone does not justify the countably infinite sum above. Removing invariance changes the question: for example, the point mass P(A)=𝟏{0∈A}P(A)=\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}} is a countably additive probability on every subset of [0,1)[0,1), but it is not rotation invariant.
The selection of VV uses the axiom of choice; the argument does not give a membership rule for VV. No restriction proved here prevents assigning probabilities to the Borel events used in this course. Intervals, disks, angular sectors and the sampling-map preimages in Section 3 are measurable. The construction explains a boundary of the all-subsets approach; it is not needed to carry out the practical calculations in the main lesson.
